strengths: Innovative and intuitive problem reformulation: Framing GUI grounding as an interactive cursor-positioning search task effectively bridges the gap between discrete numerical coordinate generation and spatial visual reasoning via explicit visual feedback.

Well-designed reinforcement learning framework: The dense trajectory reward combining the SE-GUI distance metric with four targeted behavioral penalties (false stop, false move, false direction, repeated position) prevents degenerate search behaviors and stabilizes multi-turn RL training.

Strong and convincing empirical performance: Across multiple challenging benchmarks (ScreenSpot-Pro, ScreenSpot-v2, OSWorld-G, UI-Vision, and end-to-end OSWorld agentic tasks), GUI-CURSOR substantially outperforms competitive RL and SFT baselines (e.g., outperforming GTA1-7B by 8.0% on ScreenSpot-Pro) while requiring significantly fewer training examples (8K vs. 64K).

Thorough analysis and probing of spatial capabilities: The paper includes rigorous diagnostic experiments, such as the cursor-in-box test and zero-shot spatial evaluations (SPHERE and SpatialMQA), which convincingly show that cursor-based RL instills genuine spatial reasoning rather than superficial pattern matching.

Comprehensive ablation and efficiency analysis: The paper carefully ablates the contribution of each reward penalty, thinking tokens, and the Cursor-Centric Focusing (CCF) mechanism, alongside transparent latency, throughput, and training dynamics reporting.
weaknesses: Dependence on initial prediction for Cursor-Centric Focusing (CCF): On ultra-high-resolution screenshots, CCF relies on an initial single-step prediction to define the crop area. As acknowledged in Appendix J, when the initial prediction is off-target (~10.3% of ScreenSpot-Pro instances), the model currently lacks a robust mechanism to zoom out or recover from an out-of-crop situation.

Inference latency overhead: While the majority of cases terminate within 1–2 steps, multi-step interactive grounding and image rendering inherently introduce extra latency (e.g., ~0.89s vs. 0.58s on ScreenSpot-Pro), which could become non-trivial when incorporated into high-frequency agent interaction loops.

Limited evaluation on continuous/multi-point actions: The current formulation is predominantly validated on point-and-click tasks. While extensions to continuous actions like drag-and-drop are discussed in Appendix L, empirical verification on continuous GUI interactions remains left for future work.

strengths: Reframing GUI grounding as an interactive cursor-positioning process with visual feedback provides a clear and principled solution to the known spatial semantic alignment problem in vision-language models.

The trajectory-based reward modeling is well thought out; ablations (Figure 2) clearly show that specific penalties (false stop, false move, false direction, repeated position) are crucial for preventing policy collapse and enabling effective multi-step refinement.

Strong and comprehensive empirical evaluation across static benchmarks (ScreenSpot-Pro, ScreenSpot-v2, OSWorld-G, UI-Vision) and online agentic settings (OSWorld), consistently outperforming strong baselines like GTA1 and UI-TARS while using significantly fewer training samples (8K vs. 64K+).

Thorough diagnostics and probing experiments, such as the 'cursor-in-box' task and evaluations on out-of-distribution spatial reasoning benchmarks (SPHERE and SpatialMQA), convincingly substantiate the claim that the model acquires improved spatial understanding rather than mere surface-level pattern matching.

The paper is very well documented with extensive analyses, including runtime latency, training dynamics, comparison against concurrent iterative cropping/test-time scaling methods, and transparent discussion of edge cases (e.g., target occlusion and out-of-crop initialization).
weaknesses: The cursor-centric focusing (CCF) mechanism relies heavily on the initial coarse prediction; as acknowledged in Appendix J, approximately 10.3% of ScreenSpot-Pro targets fall outside the initial crop, and the current system lacks an effective mechanism to zoom out or recover from such initialization failures.

During inference, true multi-step cursor adjustment occurs on only a small minority of test cases (only 9.4% on ScreenSpot-Pro and 0.5% on ScreenSpot-v2), indicating that much of the operational gain stems from improved one-step prediction induced by the training paradigm and CCF rather than dynamic multi-step search at test time.

Multi-step rollout during GRPO training introduces substantial computational overhead, requiring up to 680 seconds per training step compared to 289 seconds for single-step baselines, which may limit scalability when extending to larger action horizons or higher-resolution inputs.

strengths: Novel and intuitive problem formulation: Reframing GUI grounding from static one-step coordinate prediction to an interactive, cursor-driven search with visual feedback directly addresses the spatial-semantic alignment bottleneck in vision-language models.

Well-designed reinforcement learning framework: The combination of a dense distance-to-target reward with four trajectory penalties (False Stop, False Move, False Direction, Repeated Position) effectively curbs degenerate behaviors (such as premature stopping or oscillating) and stabilizes multi-step RL training with GRPO.

Strong empirical performance and sample efficiency: GUI-CURSOR achieves state-of-the-art results across prominent GUI benchmarks (e.g., +8.0% over GTA1-7B on ScreenSpot-Pro) while requiring significantly fewer training samples (8K vs. 64K).

In-depth analysis and generalisation studies: The paper provides rich analytical insights, including a minimalist cursor-in-box probing diagnostic, correlation between target size and search steps, and empirical evidence showing that visual feedback training transfers to out-of-distribution spatial reasoning benchmarks (SPHERE and SpatialMQA).
weaknesses: Inference latency and compute overhead: The multi-step interaction and image rendering naturally introduce wall-clock latency overhead (e.g., ~0.89s vs. 0.58s per sample on ScreenSpot-Pro), which could compound in full-scale online agent pipelines with long task horizons.

Brittleness to initial prediction in Cursor-Centric Focusing (CCF): CCF relies on the coarse full-image prediction landing near the target. As acknowledged in the appendix, the target falls outside the cropped window in ~10.3% of ScreenSpot-Pro cases, and the model currently lacks an effective mechanism to re-center or recover when cropped out.

Scope limited to single-point clicks: Current grounding benchmarks and the proposed trajectory environment primarily evaluate discrete click actions, leaving continuous multi-point interactions (such as drag-and-drop or drawing) without empirical validation.

strengths: Novel and intuitive problem reformulation: Reframing GUI grounding from static one-step coordinate regression to an interactive cursor-navigation task with explicit visual feedback provides a natural inductive bias for spatial grounding in VLMs.

Strong empirical performance: GUI-CURSOR achieves impressive results across major benchmarks, reaching 93.9% on ScreenSpot-v2 and notably improving performance on the challenging high-resolution ScreenSpot-Pro benchmark (56.5%, outperforming the prior leading method GTA1 at 50.1%).

Well-designed trajectory reward and comprehensive ablations: The decomposition of the reward into position proximity and four specific trajectory penalties (False Stop, False Move, False Direction, Repeated Position) is sound, with ablation studies in Section 3.2 clearly demonstrating the necessity of each penalty term in preventing degenerate search policies.

Insightful analysis and diagnostic experiments: The paper provides thorough investigations into model behavior, including analyzing step count versus target size (showing adaptive computation on smaller UI elements), multi-phase training dynamics, zero-shot multi-step limitations in base models, and the synthetic 'cursor-in-box' probe revealing spatial reasoning improvements.
weaknesses: Disentanglement of CCF (zooming/cropping) vs. interactive cursor feedback: A significant portion of the gains on ScreenSpot-Pro stems from Cursor-Centric Focusing (CCF), which improves accuracy from 45.3% to 56.5%. When CCF is removed, GUI-CURSOR lags behind GTA1 (45.3% vs. 50.1%). While GTA1 with focus achieves 54.0%, the interaction between high-resolution patch cropping and multi-step cursor reasoning could be more thoroughly disentangled.

Limited activation of multi-step search at test time: The model converges to single-step predictions for over 90% of instances in ScreenSpot-Pro and 99.5% in ScreenSpot-v2. While the authors interpret this as computational efficiency, it raises questions about whether the test-time visual feedback loop is genuinely driving performance for the vast majority of cases, or if the interactive environment primarily acts as an effective training-time curriculum/regularizer.

Evaluation scope restricted to static grounding benchmarks: The method is validated purely on isolated screenshot grounding datasets (ScreenSpot-v2 and ScreenSpot-Pro). In practical end-to-end GUI agent environments (e.g., OSWorld, WebArena), actual cursor movement triggers dynamic interface feedback (hover states, dropdowns, tooltips), which are absent in this offline rendered cursor setting.

strengths: Compelling conceptual reframing: Reformulating GUI grounding from one-step static coordinate generation into an interactive search task with rendered visual feedback (a virtual cursor) is intuitive, well-motivated, and directly tackles the spatial-semantic alignment bottleneck in VLMs.

Strong empirical results: GUI-CURSOR achieves impressive gains on established benchmarks, notably reaching 56.5% on ScreenSpot-Pro (+6.4% over the prior state-of-the-art GTA1) and 93.9% on ScreenSpot-v2, with consistent improvements across diverse domains (CAD, OS, Office).

Effective RL reward design and ablation: The trajectory-aware penalties (false stop, false move, false direction, repeated position) are well-crafted to prevent policy degeneration (e.g., trivial early stopping or oscillation), and the ablations clearly demonstrate the necessity of each component.

Insightful probing and analysis: The minimalist 'cursor-in-box' diagnostic experiment cleanly reveals the base model's spatial center bias and demonstrates that trajectory-based RL improves generalized spatial reasoning without explicit supervision on the probing task.

Pragmatic multi-resolution strategy: The Cursor-Centric Focusing (CCF) approach neatly resolves the dilemma between the computational expense of training on native ultra-high-resolution screenshots and the need for fine-grained inference on small UI elements.
weaknesses: Lack of end-to-end agent evaluation: The evaluation is restricted to standalone GUI grounding benchmarks (ScreenSpot-v2 and ScreenSpot-Pro). Demonstrating how this interactive grounding policy integrates into full multi-turn GUI agents (e.g., OSWorld, Mind2Web, or WebArena) would substantiate its broader system-level value.

Failure mode in Cursor-Centric Focusing: If the initial coarse step prediction lands far from the target UI element, the cropped window completely excludes the target (reported as occurring in 10.3% of ScreenSpot-Pro instances), and the current framework lacks a mechanism to zoom out or recover from an out-of-frame crop.

Evaluation on a single base model architecture: The fine-tuning experiments rely exclusively on Qwen2.5-VL-7B. Evaluating across different model scales (e.g., 2B/3B models) or alternative VLM families would strengthen claims regarding the generality of the RL framework.

Missing latency and inference computational overhead analysis: While the paper notes that ~95% of instances terminate within two steps, multi-step generation combined with cropping increases wall-clock latency, token usage, and visual encoding overhead compared to single-step baselines, which warrants explicit reporting.

strengths: Novel and intuitive problem formulation: Reframing static GUI visual grounding into an interactive cursor-navigation task with explicit visual feedback effectively addresses the spatial semantic misalignment commonly faced by vision-language models.

Strong empirical performance: GUI-CURSOR achieves state-of-the-art results on both ScreenSpot-v2 (93.9%) and ScreenSpot-Pro (56.5%), notably outperforming the prior leading model GTA1 by +6.4% on the challenging high-resolution ScreenSpot-Pro benchmark.

Well-designed trajectory reward modeling: The inclusion of trajectory-level penalties (false stop, false move, false direction, and repeated position) is soundly motivated and empirically validated to prevent policy collapse into degenerate single-step behaviors.

Thorough empirical analysis and probing: The paper provides insightful diagnostic experiments, such as the cursor-in-box spatial reasoning probing test revealing the base model's positional center-bias, and detailed analysis correlating movement steps with UI target size.

Practical efficiency considerations: The combination of downscaled training with inference-time Cursor-Centric Focusing (CCF) offers an effective balance between training throughput and high-resolution inference accuracy.
weaknesses: Error propagation in Cursor-Centric Focusing (CCF): If the first coarse grounding step misses the target by a large margin, the cropped window fails to contain the target (affecting ~10.3% of ScreenSpot-Pro samples as noted in Appendix B.5), leading to an unrecoverable failure mode.

Inference latency and computational overhead: While most instances resolve within one or two turns, generating multi-turn reasoning traces alongside re-rendering screenshots incurs additional inference cost compared to standard single-pass feedforward grounding.

Evaluation restricted to static grounding benchmarks: The method is validated purely on isolated grounding datasets (ScreenSpot-v2 and ScreenSpot-Pro); evaluating integration within full downstream GUI agent benchmarks (e.g., OSWorld or Mind2Web) would further demonstrate practical utility.
